critical_code_review_comments: server.py has grown to 951 lines and now clearly exceeds the 700-line file-size guideline. Auth (Google + JWT + reset + brute force), public content, patient CRUD, labs, messaging, doctor notes, admin, AI, and seed are all in a single module. Please split into routers/modules (auth_email.py, auth_google.py, patient.py, labs.py, messages.py, doctor.py, admin.py, ai.py, seed.py).

logger is defined at module bottom (line 897) but referenced from function bodies earlier (forgot_password line 367, ai_assessment line 796). This works only because the functions are called at request time, after module import completes. It is a footgun — future refactors that call these at import time will break. Move logging.basicConfig + logger definition to the top of the file (right after imports).

Brute-force lockout keyed by request.client.host+email is fragile behind Kubernetes ingress: the ingress balances requests across backend pods AND the client IP the server sees can rotate between two internal proxy IPs. A single attacker easily gets 2x-3x the allotted attempts before either identifier reaches 5. Consider (a) using X-Forwarded-For (first hop) instead of client.host, and (b) also tracking failures per-email globally, not just per (ip,email).

login_attempts.identifier has unique index but the doc is created with upsert on first fail. If two parallel fails race, one upsert will conflict on the unique index and raise DuplicateKeyError (uncaught → 500 to client). Use $inc with upsert=True instead of read-modify-write.

clear_auth_cookies uses response.delete_cookie(name, path='/') but the cookies were set with samesite='none' and secure=True. Some browsers require the deletion Set-Cookie to also carry samesite=none; secure to actually clear. Consider setting them to empty with max_age=0 + same attributes for maximum compatibility.

Register endpoint auto-promotes a Google-only user (no password_hash) to a password-holder without any verification of ownership. If Google user A had signed up before, anyone knowing A's email can register a password and hijack their account. Recommend either (a) forbid register when a user exists without password_hash (return 409 with a 'sign in with Google and set a password from settings' message) or (b) send a confirmation email to the address before attaching a password.

/auth/refresh only rotates access_token but not refresh_token (no refresh-token rotation). Long-lived refresh tokens without rotation are the typical attack vector for stolen tokens; industry-standard is to also rotate the refresh_token on each /refresh and revoke the old one.
/auth/forgot-password does not enforce any rate limit — an attacker can hammer it to fill password_reset_tokens (TTL indexed but still bloat). Add a small per-email throttle.

get_current_user swallows both ExpiredSignatureError and InvalidTokenError silently and falls through to the session_token path. An expired JWT should probably surface a 401 with 'token expired' so the frontend can call /auth/refresh, instead of masquerading as 'not authenticated' after the fallback also fails.

Frontend: after login/register success, Login.jsx calls await refresh() and then nav(...). But AuthContext.refresh sets loading=false only inside .finally, and Login's useEffect that navigates on user+!loading may fire a second navigation. Not a functional bug now (both go to same route) but could double-navigate in edge cases. Consider only navigating from doSignIn/doSignUp and dropping the useEffect redirect for freshly signed-in users.

Frontend: /login redirects an already-logged-in user to their dashboard, but the redirect happens in a useEffect after render — for a split-second the sign-in form flashes. Consider returning null (or a spinner) while loading || user is truthy.
